<reason>A very close, high-quality debate. CON built a coherent frame (the motion is about crated animals with a government logo; consent is the mechanism by which the ecology survives) and landed two strong, unanswered points: the lynx/roe-vs-red-deer mismatch and the verification asymmetry favouring outcome-based culling. But CON's central empirical claim—that imposed predators simply die—was directly tested by its own pressure question, and PRO answered it squarely with Yellowstone, Swiss lynx and Scottish sea eagles. CON dismissed Yellowstone plausibly and turned Switzerland into a cost story, but ignored the sea eagles entirely. CON's sequencing answer ("build coexistence around wolves that walk in, then release") also collides with CON's own emphasis that Scotland is an island where nothing walks in, which PRO's "locked door with the key inside" exploited. PRO's closing then converted CON's consent definition into "a policy that returns no by construction" and "release where predators are least needed"—neither of which CON's closing answered. PRO's misstep in claiming its question was "unanswered" before CON had a turn is a real execution cost, and PRO never addressed the verification-asymmetry or lynx-mismatch points, keeping the margin thin. On balance PRO's route—herbivore problem conceded, impositions demonstrably persist at a cost, veto structurally forecloses action—survived slightly more intact.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The pressure-question exchange: CON demanded one deliberate release over sustained objection that established without the community coming round; PRO named Yellowstone, Swiss lynx and Scottish sea eagles and reframed the question as demanding a precondition (acceptance) that only coexistence produces. CON's counter—Yellowstone is federal land with a continental reservoir, Switzerland proves "the price of imposition"—was sharp but left sea eagles untouched and conceded the animals persisted.</best_rebuttal>
